name: Learning from rewards and feedback
gist: Papers using reinforcement learning and reward-shaping techniques to train robots to improve their behavior through trial and error—the challenge is defining useful reward signals and making learning stable.
explain: Another way to teach robots is to let them learn by trial and error, the way a child learns to walk or throw a ball. You define a reward—a number that tells the robot how well it did. If the goal is to pick up a cup, the robot gets a high reward when it touches the cup, and a higher reward when it grasps it. The robot tries many different actions, and over time, it learns which actions lead to higher rewards. This is called reinforcement learning. The appeal is that you do not have to provide demonstrations; you just have to define what success looks like. The robot will figure out its own way to get there.

The challenge is defining a useful reward signal and making the learning stable. If the reward is too simple ('just grab the object'), the robot learns a brittle policy that works in one exact situation but fails if the object is slightly different or in a different place. If the reward is complex, you have to specify dozens of details, and robots optimize the reward you gave them, not the goal you intended. Worse, reinforcement learning is slow. A robot in the real world cannot try 10,000 failed actions to learn one good skill—each failure is costly, and each trial takes time. So researchers try to speed it up using simulation, where they can run thousands of trials per second. But then the robot learns in simulation, and when you put it in the real world, the physics is slightly different and the policy fails. This 'reality gap' is enormous in robotics.

Papers here tackle the problem from multiple angles. Some use reward shaping—giving the robot intermediate rewards for progress, so it learns faster. Some use hierarchical learning—teaching the robot to learn simple skills first (grasp), then build on them (grasp and lift). Others use feedback from humans—as the robot learns, a person occasionally corrects it or gives it hints, speeding up learning massively. Some work to bridge the reality gap by training in simulation in a way that the learned policy transfers better to real robots. A few use prediction as a shortcut: instead of learning what reward a real action gives, the robot learns to predict what will happen, and uses that prediction to pick actions without actually trying them as many times.

papers.title: AnyTouch 2: General Optical Tactile Representation Learning For Dynamic Tactile Perception
papers.contribution: Presents the first comprehensive hierarchical dynamic tactile perception ecosystem combining systematic data collection and multi-level model design for force-aware object manipulation.

papers.title: BFM-Zero: A Promptable Behavioral Foundation Model for Humanoid Control Using Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
papers.contribution: Demonstrates zero-shot motion tracking, goal reaching, reward inference, and few-shot adaptation on Unitree G1 humanoid in real world.

papers.title: Cerebellar-Inspired Residual Control for Fault Recovery: From Inference-Time Adaptation to Structural Consolidation
papers.contribution: Achieves up to +66% improvement on HalfCheetah-v5 and +53% on Humanoid-v5 under moderate faults with graceful degradation under severe shifts.

papers.title: Contact-guided Real2Sim from Monocular Video with Planar Scene Primitives
papers.contribution: Reduces motion-tracking failure rates from 55.2% to 6.9% on EMDB and PROX benchmarks while delivering 43% faster RL simulation throughput for robotics applications.

papers.title: Demystifying Robot Diffusion Policies: Action Memorization and a Simple Lookup Table Alternative
papers.contribution: Provides systematic empirical evidence showing diffusion policy outputs training action chunks even for OOD images; proposes ALT lookup table policy as alternative.

papers.title: ExoPredicator: Learning Abstract Models of Dynamic Worlds for Robot Planning
papers.contribution: The learned models enable fast planning that generalizes to held-out tasks with more objects and more complex goals, outperforming baselines on five simulated tabletop robotics environments.

papers.title: From Seeing to Experiencing: Scaling Navigation Foundation Models with Reinforcement Learning
papers.contribution: S2E maintains generalizability from large-scale pretraining while enhancing interactivity through RL, achieving state-of-the-art performance on NavBench-GS and real-world robustness assessments.

papers.title: Model Predictive Adversarial Imitation Learning for Planning from Observation
papers.contribution: A common paradigm for learning how to plan-from-demonstration involves first solving for a reward via Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) and then deploying it via Model Predictive Control (MPC).

papers.title: OVSeg3R: Learn Open-vocabulary Instance Segmentation from 2D via 3D Reconstruction
papers.contribution: By exploiting the 2D to 3D correspondences provided by 3D reconstruction models, OVSeg3R projects each view's 2D instance mask predictions, obtained from an open-vocabulary 2D model, onto 3D to generate annotations for the view's corresponding sub-scene.

papers.title: Sparse Imagination for Efficient Visual World Model Planning
papers.contribution: Sparse imagination maintains task performance while dramatically improving inference efficiency, enabling deployment of world models in real-time robotics scenarios.

papers.title: TrajTok: What makes for a good trajectory tokenizer in behavior generation?

papers.title: A Schrödinger Eigenfunction Method for Long-Horizon Stochastic Optimal Control

papers.title: APPLE: Toward General Active Perception via Reinforcement Learning
papers.contribution: Achieves high accuracies on Tactile MNIST and other tasks, demonstrating versatility as general framework for active perception.

papers.title: AdaNav: Adaptive Reasoning with Uncertainty for Vision-Language Navigation
